topic.title: Why You See Halos Around Lights
topic.audience_question: Why do lights sometimes develop glowing rings, and when can a halo signal an eye emergency?
topic.pubmed_query: halos around lights glare tear film cataract corneal edema acute angle closure glaucoma

sources.title: Cataracts
sources.abstract: The National Eye Institute explains that cataracts cloud the natural lens and may cause blurry or hazy vision, faded colors, poor night vision, glare, and halos around lights. Diagnosis uses a comprehensive dilated eye examination.

sources.title: Glaucoma
sources.abstract: The National Eye Institute states that angle-closure glaucoma can produce sudden intense eye pain, nausea, a red eye, and blurry vision. These symptoms require immediate assessment by a doctor or emergency department.

sources.title: Understanding Glaucoma: Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis, Treatment
sources.abstract: The American Academy of Ophthalmology describes angle-closure attacks as involving severe eye or forehead pain, eye redness, reduced or blurred vision, rainbow-colored halos, headache, nausea, and vomiting, and identifies the condition as an emergency.

sources.title: Dry Eye
sources.abstract: The National Eye Institute explains that dry eye occurs when tears are insufficient or do not work correctly. An unstable ocular surface may cause burning, scratchiness, light sensitivity, and blurred or fluctuating vision.

sources.title: Corneal Edema
sources.abstract: This American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki review defines corneal edema as fluid accumulation that thickens the cornea and reduces transparency. Causes include endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, trauma, surgery, and raised eye pressure, with slit-lamp examination and corneal measurements helping identify the cause.

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Acanthamoeba Keratitis
sources.abstract: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention describes Acanthamoeba keratitis as a rare but serious corneal infection associated especially with contact-lens wear. Symptoms may include eye pain, redness, blurred vision, light sensitivity, excessive tearing, and a foreign-body sensation, and early diagnosis improves the chance of effective treatment.
sources.journal: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: TFOS DEWS III: Diagnostic Methodology
sources.abstract: This international consensus report recommends assessing dry-eye symptoms together with objective tear-film and ocular-surface findings, examining the eyelids and tear film, identifying risk factors, and considering alternative diagnoses rather than relying on symptoms alone.

episode.title: E44: Why You See Halos Around Lights
episode.hook: Hello and welcome to the Your Only Doc podcast. Imagine driving after sunset. Every headlight has a glowing ring, and street lamps look smeared. You blink, clean your glasses, and wonder whether this is normal. A halo is not a diagnosis. It is a clue that light is being scattered before the image reaches the retina. The pattern, timing, and other symptoms tell us whether the cause is simple, gradual, or urgent.

sections.heading: The high yield summary
sections.narration: Too busy? Here is your high yield summary. Halos can come from an unstable tear film, an outdated glasses prescription, cataract, corneal swelling, infection, or sudden pressure rise inside the eye. Notice whether blinking clears them, whether one eye is worse, and whether the change is gradual or sudden. Stop driving if vision is unsafe. New rainbow halos with severe eye pain, redness, headache, nausea, vomiting, or sudden blur can mean angle-closure glaucoma and require emergency care now.
on_screen: A halo is a light-scattering clue
Painful red eye is an emergency

sections.heading: Why a ring forms around a light
sections.narration: A clear optical system should focus light sharply. When the tear film is irregular, the cornea is swollen, the lens is cloudy, or focus is imperfect, some light spreads across the retina instead. Bright points against a dark background make this scatter especially noticeable. That is why halos often appear around headlights at night. Large pupils in darkness also expose more of the eye's optical imperfections. The shape alone cannot reliably identify the cause.

sections.heading: Blinking can reveal a tear-film problem
sections.narration: The tear film is the first focusing surface light meets. If it breaks up unevenly, vision can fluctuate and lights may flare or smear. A few complete blinks may briefly sharpen the image before it blurs again. Burning, grittiness, watering, screen use, wind, air conditioning, and contact lenses support this possibility. But temporary improvement with blinking is only a clue. Persistent symptoms still need examination because dry eye and corneal disease can feel similar.

sections.heading: Focus and glasses matter at night
sections.narration: Nearsightedness, astigmatism, a changing prescription, dirty lenses, or poorly fitting contact lenses can spread light. The problem may be most obvious while night driving even when daytime vision seems acceptable. Clean the lenses, compare each eye separately, and arrange a proper refraction if the symptom continues. Do not test yourself by driving farther. If signs, pedestrians, or lane markings are hard to see, stop in a safe place and use another way home.
on_screen: Compare one eye at a time
Do not drive with unsafe vision

sections.heading: Cataracts usually change vision gradually
sections.narration: A cataract clouds the natural lens and scatters incoming light. Halos often arrive with glare, faded colors, hazy vision, poor night vision, or frequent prescription changes. The progression is commonly slow and painless, so people may first notice that driving after dark has become uncomfortable. Cataracts are diagnosed with a dilated eye examination. Surgery is considered when the cataract interferes with daily activities, not merely because a halo appears once.
on_screen: Glare and poor night vision are common

sections.heading: The cornea can become cloudy or swollen
sections.narration: The cornea must stay transparent. Fluid accumulation, inflammation, injury, surgery, inherited endothelial disease, or infection can disturb that clarity and create blur, glare, and halos. Pain, redness, light sensitivity, tearing, or a foreign-body feeling makes a surface problem more concerning. Contact-lens wearers should remove the lens and seek prompt eye care for pain or redness. Do not place the lens back in or use leftover steroid drops, because a corneal infection can worsen quickly.
on_screen: Pain and redness need prompt care

sections.heading: Rainbow halos can signal a pressure emergency
sections.narration: Acute angle closure is uncommon, but missing it can cost vision. Pressure can rise rapidly when fluid cannot leave the front of the eye. The warning pattern is a sudden painful red eye with blurred vision, rainbow-colored halos, headache, nausea, or vomiting. Do not sleep on it, drive yourself, or wait for a routine appointment. Go to an emergency department or urgent eye service immediately. A painless halo without those symptoms is different, but a new persistent change still deserves assessment.

sections.heading: How an eye examination finds the cause
sections.narration: Now, let us go deeper. The clinician checks visual acuity and refraction, examines the tear film and cornea with a slit lamp, measures eye pressure, and looks through the pupil at the lens and retina. Corneal staining or thickness measurements may be useful. The history should include timing, one eye or both, contact lenses, previous surgery, medicines, trauma, and whether blinking changes the halo. These details separate surface instability from lens clouding, corneal edema, and pressure-related disease.

sections.heading: Three essential takeaways
sections.narration: Number one, halos mean light is scattering, and common causes include tear-film instability, focus problems, and cataract. Number two, note whether blinking helps, whether one eye differs, how quickly the change began, and whether pain, redness, or nausea is present. Number three, stop driving when vision is unsafe, arrange an eye examination for a new or persistent halo, and treat sudden rainbow halos with a painful red eye, headache, nausea, vomiting, or sudden blur as an emergency.
on_screen: Act urgently on the painful red eye

episode.closing: On the next episode, we will explain why your pupils can look different sizes, which differences are harmless, and which combinations need urgent neurological or eye assessment. Until then, never let a halo with pain and redness wait until morning.
episode.description: Halos around lights can come from tear-film instability, focus problems, cataract, corneal swelling, infection, or acute angle closure. This episode explains how timing, blinking, one-eye comparison, pain, redness, and nausea help separate routine causes from an eye emergency.
